title: Sin is behovely (ch. 27)
hook: sin was necessary, she says, but all shall be well
tomorrow: what if you fall while you're running to help?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Julian's Mother Jesus, who feeds us with himself and holds us close. The line was mother Jesus.

It's the question that turns up at two in the morning, at a hospital bedside, in the comments under a hard headline. If God is good and able, why not stop the bad thing before it starts? Julian of Norwich asks it straight out, about sin itself. The answer she receives doesn't explain as much as it promises.
screen: `THE TWO A.M. QUESTION.` → `WHY NOT STOP IT FIRST?` → `A PROMISE, NOT AN EXPLANATION.`

segments.voice: In chapter twenty-seven, Julian wonders why God, in his great wisdom, didn't prevent sin's beginning. Then, she thinks, all would have been well. The first half of the answer: sin is behovely. It's an old English word readers gloss as fitting, or needed, something with its place. She doesn't call sin good. She says she never saw sin itself; it has no substance of its own, and she knew it only by the pain it causes. The second half, in Grace Warrack's edition: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." She isn't told how. And he says it, she writes, very tenderly, with no blame toward her, nor toward any who will be saved. A promise said more than once, to someone weighed down, is something another tradition knows too. In the Qur'an, a short surah speaks to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and repeats itself. In Pickthall's translation: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." Muslims receive those words as God's own. Here's the honest difference. The surah speaks of hardship and the ease that comes with it. Julian's promise is about sin itself, and for her it's Jesus who speaks it. Two different voices, each repeating the promise so it can be heard.
screen: `WHY NOT STOP SIN FIRST?` · `BEHOVELY: IT HAS ITS PLACE.` · `ALL SHALL BE WELL, SAID TENDERLY.` · `WITH HARDSHIP GOETH EASE.` · then, large: `ALL MANNER OF THING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one failure you still carry. Don't argue for it or against it; set Julian's line beside it, all shall be well, and leave the how alone. Anyone who prays can hand that one thing to God until the sit ends.
Sin is behovely. Julian's hard word: sin has its place, and still all shall be well.
Your line: all manner of thing. Not some things, but all manner of thing shall be well. Sleep well.

howItsDone: Some Catholics pray with Julian's 'all shall be well' in times of worry; her book is read as devotion, alongside the Church's teaching on sin and redemption.

'A short surah speaks to the Prophet Muhammad' rests on the surah's second-person address (94:1 'Have We not caused thy bosom to dilate'); confirm the framing with a Muslim scholar. The shared thing (a repeated promise to someone weighed down) and the honest difference (hardship and ease vs. sin itself, spoken by Jesus for Julian) are stated without ranking; no claim that the two mean the same.
The myth item 'nothing bad will happen' is the popular misreading of 'all shall be well'.
